name: Ear coning (thermal-auricular therapy)

card.summary: Ear coning is the practice of burning a hollow wax-and-fabric cone at the ear opening, marketed for earwax removal and a clean, relaxed feeling in the ears and head.
card.aka: ear candling; thermal-auricular therapy; auricular candles
card.note: The FDA and Health Canada warn of burns, wax blockage and eardrum injury; clinicians advise other wax-removal methods.

quick.overview:
Ear coning, or ear candling, involves placing the narrow end of a hollow candle-like cone in the ear while the other end burns. Practitioners and marketers present it for removing earwax and for general well-being.

The appearance link is grooming: people use it for ear cleanliness and a relaxing spa-style ritual. Studies have not found that the cones remove wax, and regulators warn about injuries, so clinicians point to other methods for earwax.
quick.how: In spa and home settings, the person lies on one side while a cone is held in the ear and burned for roughly ten to twenty minutes, with a paper, foil or plastic shield around the ear and hair. Some people combine it with facial or head massage.
quick.risks: Burns are the most commonly reported injury, and wax blockage and eardrum perforation have also been reported. The FDA says it is dangerous when used as labeled, and Health Canada calls it dangerous especially for children. At least two house fires, one fatal, have been linked to candling accidents.

lead: Ear coning, also called ear candling or thermal-auricular therapy, is an alternative practice in which a hollow cone made of fabric and wax is lit at one end while the other end rests at the ear canal opening [1]. Practitioners say the flame creates suction that draws out earwax and impurities and promotes well-being [1].

People use it for the grooming and relaxation side of looks: clean ears, a spa ritual and a feeling of lightness around the head. The debris seen after a session is described by researchers as candle wax and soot, which candles also leave when burned outside the ear [1].

Medical bodies have examined it. A 1996 clinic study found the candles generated no negative pressure and did not remove wax, and reviews in 2004 and 2007 found no reliable evidence of benefit [1]. The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery guideline on earwax discusses evidence-based management of cerumen impaction and lists interventions it considers contraindicated [2][3].

chain: Cone burns at the ear opening
angle.text: Ear coning is promoted for earwax removal and relaxation. Tested in clinics, the candles did not draw out wax, so the result users see is cone residue and the experience itself.

Marketed as Hopi; the Hopi Tribal Council says it is not Hopi tradition [1]

paras: The person lies on their side with the cone in the ear, and a paper, foil or plastic cover protects the face and hair. The cone burns for about 10 to 20 minutes [1].

A manufacturer marketed its candles as Hopi ear candles, but the Hopi Tribal Council has said the practice was never part of Hopi tradition. Chinese, Egyptian, North American and Atlantean origins have also been claimed without documentation, and the earliest records place its development in 20th-century Arizona [1].

A 1996 study at a Spokane ear clinic found no negative pressure and no wax removal [1]. Edzard Ernst's 2004 review stated there is no data to suggest it is effective for any condition, and a 2007 Canadian Family Physician paper recommended that doctors discourage use [1]. One trial cited in a 2007 American Family Physician article found candles caused wax blockage [1].
The 2017 AAO-HNSF guideline update on earwax provides recommendations on hygiene, diagnosis and treatment of cerumen impaction [2][3].

The FDA issued an alert in 2007 saying ear candles are dangerous when used as labeled and that selling them with medical claims is illegal. Health Canada found no proof of benefit and states there is plenty of proof of danger, particularly for children [1]. ENT surgeons report burns as the most common complication, with wax blockage and eardrum perforation also documented [1].

No studies found showing that ear candles remove earwax or improve health. Studies that have tested them report no negative pressure or wax removal [1]; broader earwax management guidelines are summarized by the AAO-HNSF [2][3].
